models.collectorNote: Early flat-floor, outside-bonnet-latch Series 1 cars top the market at auction. Buy on body condition, rust repair on the monocoque is where budgets go to die.

generations.name: Series 1
generations.note: Launched at £2,097 in the UK, half the price of an Aston Martin with the same 150 mph claim. The 4.2 of 1964 added a better gearbox and seats you could sit in all day.

generations.name: Series 2
generations.note: US safety rules drove most changes: bigger lights, a wraparound rear bumper, exposed headlights. Mechanically improved, visually diluted, and cheaper to buy today because of it.

generations.name: Series 3
generations.note: The 5.3-litre V12 made it a relaxed GT rather than a sports car, and most were automatics. Flared arches and a bigger grille finished the transformation.

models.intro: Enzo Ferrari reportedly called it the most beautiful car ever made, and he was not wrong. 150 mph for a third of an Aston's price in 1961, on a monocoque with the XK engine and independent rear suspension. The standard every GT since has been judged against.

generations.name: Series I XJ6
generations.note: William Lyons' last great design: short-deck elegance, twin fuel tanks and the XK six in 2.8 and 4.2 forms. The V12 XJ12 of 1972 was the fastest four-door in the world.

generations.name: X350
generations.note: An aluminium body under deliberately traditional styling, 40% lighter than the steel car it replaced. The supercharged XJR is the stealth pick of the whole XJ line.

generations.name: X351
generations.note: Ian Callum threw out fifty years of XJ styling in one move. All-aluminium, no six-cylinder in the US, and the long-wheelbase car became a genuine chauffeur rival. The last XJ ever, the electric successor was cancelled.

models.intro: Jaguar's flagship saloon for half a century, from William Lyons' Series I to Ian Callum's radical X351. The XJ was always the driver's luxury car, lighter, lower and keener than the German default, when it wasn't being let down by 1970s build quality.
models.name: XJ

models.collectorNote: The SVR and the manual-gearbox V6 cars are the collector ends of the range. Exhaust and rear-diff service history matters; the noise is worth it.

generations.name: First phase
generations.note: V6 and V8 supercharged engines, an aluminium body and the loudest factory exhaust this side of a race car. The SVR of 2016 pushed the V8 to 575 hp.

generations.name: Facelift
generations.note: Slimmer lights, a tidier range and the four-cylinder P300 at the bottom. Production ended in 2024, the last petrol Jaguar sports car, full stop.

models.intro: The E-Type's self-appointed heir: an aluminium two-seater with supercharged V6 and V8 engines and a crackling exhaust that became its signature. The facelift cleaned up the styling; the SVR turned it into a genuine supercar-baiter.
models.name: F-Type

models.collectorNote: Original XK120s with matching numbers and the alloy-bodied early cars lead the market. The SE 'M' specification is the driver's pick.

generations.name: Production run
generations.note: The fastest production car in the world at launch, '120' was the mph claim, and a near-stock car proved 132 mph in Belgium in 1949. About 240 early cars were alloy-bodied before steel production began.

models.intro: A show car that escaped. Jaguar built the XK120 for the 1948 London Motor Show as a showcase for its new XK engine, took hundreds of orders, and had to put it into production. It defined the British sports car for a generation and launched Jaguar's Le Mans era.
models.name: XK120
